The Florida mouse (Podomys floridanus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate that is relatively modest for a cricetid rodent of its size. Under standard thermoneutral conditions maintained at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], respirometry trials have recorded a resting oxygen consumption of 51.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 51.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the species' adaptation to the warm, xeric environments of central Florida's sand pine scrub. This metabolic measurement was obtained from post-absorptive adults during their inactive phase, ensuring that the recorded rate represents true basal metabolism rather than the elevated costs of digestion or activity. Neonates of this species are altricial at delivery, weighing only 2.4 grams [Wwb = 2.4 grams] at birth, a modest mass that underscores the extensive parental investment required during the subsequent weeks of lactation. The combination of a low basal metabolic rate and a small initial offspring mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival in an unpredictable, fire-prone landscape.

Lactation in Podomys floridanus proceeds rapidly relative to the gestation period. Under captive conditions held at a stable 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], the interval from birth to the cessation of nursing has been documented at 25 days [tx = 25 days], a duration that aligns with the weaning ages reported for other small peromyscine rodents. At this milestone, the young typically attain a wet weight at weaning of 12.5 grams [Wwx = 12.5 grams], representing a more than fivefold increase from their birth mass. Growth during the suckling period is fueled entirely by maternal milk, and the efficiency of this transfer is reflected in the substantial mass gain achieved in less than four weeks. The weaning process itself involves a gradual dietary transition from milk to solid food, with the mother provisioning cached seeds and arthropods before full nutritional independence is achieved. At a body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], puberty occurs at approximately 40 days after birth [tp = approximately 40 days after birth], a developmental schedule that allows individuals to enter the breeding population during the same season in which they were weaned. This relatively rapid maturation is complemented by a gestation period lasting 32 days [tg = 32 days] under the same thermal conditions, a duration that is typical for a rodent of this body size at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. The 32-day gestation (32 days) [tg = 32 days] includes a post-implantation phase during which organogenesis proceeds rapidly, culminating in the birth of a small litter after roughly one month at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. Reproductive output is correspondingly high, with females producing litters averaging 2.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.5 pups per litter], a fecundity that supports rapid population turnover in ephemeral habitat patches.

Captive individuals held at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C] have been documented to survive for approximately 7.4 years [am = approximately 7.4 years], though free-ranging animals rarely approach this ceiling due to predation and habitat disturbance. Under field conditions, a female typically produces 2.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.5 pups per litter] and can initiate up to two litters per year [F_R_i = up to two litters per year], yielding a modest yearly reproductive output that is offset by high adult survivorship in favorable years. This reproductive rhythm is attuned to the stochastic fire regime of Florida scrub, where post-fire succession generates pulses of seed production that fuel population irruptions. The maximum adult body mass recorded in the species is 23.4 grams [Wwi = 23.4 grams], though individuals from some populations may reach the upper end of a range extending to 36 grams.

Comparative physiological data situate the Florida mouse among the more energetically conservative members of the Neotominae subfamily. The longevity record of 7.4 years [am = 7.4 years] places Podomys floridanus among the longer-lived peromyscine rodents, a trait that may buffer populations against the demographic consequences of periodic scrub fires that remove substantial portions of the standing vegetation and reduce food availability for extended periods at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C].
